slides: Open by framing the chapter as a change of language: tensors become measuring devices, and differential forms survive coordinate changes. Emphasize that the lecture will not try to list every identity at once. The through-line is alternation, then smooth variation, then the universal derivative d.

Use the dependency map as the lecture itinerary. Point out that wedge product is not a side operation; it is the bridge from alternating algebra to forms on manifolds. The checks attached to the notebook verify that the route reaches both naturality of d and Cartan formula.

Slow down on the dimension count because it fixes a common misconception. A k-covector is not an arbitrary k-index array once alternation is imposed; increasing multi-indices are enough. The determinant example explains why repeated or dependent directions give zero volume.

Read the wedge product as an oriented measurement rather than as a symbolic multiplication rule. The displayed computation gives alpha wedge beta on u and v as a signed determinant, so swapping the two inputs reverses the sign and repeating an input kills the area.

Make the contravariance of pullback concrete: a form that lives on the target is tested by vectors from the source after applying the map. The heat map shows the same coefficient obtained from F star d omega and d F star omega, and the residual in the check file is zero.

Present d as the derivative that is forced by antisymmetry. On functions it is the ordinary differential; on one-forms it arranges partial derivatives into wedge coefficients. The product rule row is useful because it says d is still a derivation, but a graded one.

Use this slide to explain why d squared equals zero is structural rather than accidental. The second derivatives appear twice with opposite signs after antisymmetrization. The notebook checks this both for a function and for a one-form, so the diagram is backed by symbolic residuals.

Introduce interior multiplication as insertion of a vector field into the first slot of a form. Cartan formula then says the Lie derivative of a form can be computed from contraction and exterior derivative. The vector-field plot is a concrete one-form example where both residual components vanish.

Treat the learner lab as a short in-class prediction exercise. Ask students to infer from d omega equals (2 minus a) X dX wedge dY that only a equals 2 gives a closed one-form on the plane. The table then confirms why the wedge coefficient is the whole diagnostic.

Close by reconnecting the algebraic and geometric halves of the chapter. Alternation gives oriented volume, pullback gives coordinate-stable transport, d gives a canonical derivative, and Cartan formula ties d to flows. The final sanity file records these as checked artifacts rather than unsupported claims.
